extracted.intended_audience: readers and practitioners of natural philosophy / physics (scholars, students, astronomers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and methodological principles (from Newton's Author/Editor's prefaces) for producing and assessing physical theories: how to derive laws from phenomena, what kinds of hypotheses or explanations are acceptable, and the empirical/mathematical standards a successful theory must meet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer experimental philosophy over speculative scholastic or fanciful mechanistic hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Physics should be 'experimental' — derive laws from selected phenomena, not from untested occult qualities or gratuitous hypotheses. The Editor contrasts three approaches and endorses the experimental (analytic + synthetic) method as 'longe optima'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject explanations that rest on invented 'occult qualities' or on ad hoc 'subtle' matter unless their existence is demonstrated by phenomena; favour derivations from experiments and observations, followed by mathematical demonstration. Example anti-patterns: Aristotelian 'occult qualities' and unfounded Cartesian subtle-matter vortices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses are not admitted in physics except as questions
rubrics_metrics.description: As stated, 'Hypotheses non comminiscentur, neque in physicam recipiunt' — hypotheses should not be used as accepted causes in physical explanations unless they are tested; they can be posed only as questions whose truth is to be investigated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat hypothetical mechanisms as established explanations; use them only to form testable questions and then seek confirmation by observation/experiment. Scoring note: theories that rest principally on untested hypotheses score poorly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic then synthetic method (derive laws from phenomena, then deduce consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceed by analysis: from selected phenomena deduce the simplest forces/laws; then by synthesis reconstruct the system and deduce further phenomena mathematically. This is the praised procedure in the preface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis: identify simple causes from observed facts. Synthesis: demonstrate how those causes produce the full range of phenomena. Example: Newton deduces gravitational laws from planetary/ lunar/pendulum observations, then synthesizes to derive planetary motions and tides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical demonstration is required for physical propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical propositions should be proposed and demonstrated mathematically ('mathesin excolere... quatenus ea ad philosophiam spectat').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise mathematical reasoning to show that proposed laws imply observed phenomena (areas proportional to times, orbital shapes, periods). Theories lacking rigorous mathematical demonstration are inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parsimony / simplicity of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer the simplest set of causes that suffice to explain phenomena; avoid inventing numerous, complex, or hidden causes when simpler explanations (fewer causes) suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple hypotheses explain phenomena, prefer the one with fewer assumptions and with demonstrable consequences. Anti-pattern: positing many fictitious causes (e.g., complex systems of vortices) to 'save the appearances.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality / universality of laws from local phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles inferred from observed phenomena in one region (e.g., Europe) should be generalized to nature at large unless there is evidence to the contrary: 'Quis enim dubitat... eadem sit causa... in America?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the rule that similar kinds of effects with similar properties have the same causes everywhere; this justifies extending terrestrial experiment-based inferences to celestial bodies. Limitations must be justified by observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require empirical confirmation (experiments & astronomical observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws and theories must be confirmed by experiments (pendulums, falling bodies) and by astronomical observations (planetary motions, comets, lunar inequalities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrations should be checked against experimental data (e.g., pendulum isochronism, free-fall accelerations) and precise astronomical measurements (periods, distances, apsidal motion). The preface cites pendulum experiments, lunar motion, cometary observations as key confirmations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject speculative media or vortices that cannot account for observed variety of motions
rubrics_metrics.description: Vortex or continuous-fluid hypotheses are rejected because they cannot plausibly produce the observed variety of planetary and cometary velocities, eccentricities, and orbital forms without implausible assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explanatory mechanism must account for varying speeds, different orbital determinations, and long-term stability; if a mechanism requires ad hoc and complex modifications, it should be discarded. Example: the text argues vortices cannot explain differing planet velocities at the same solar distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forces must be composable from parts (additivity / composition principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The action of a body is to be composed of the attractions of its parts: 'Actio... ex conjunctis partium actionibus confari censenda erit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When computing forces between extended bodies, treat the total attraction as the sum (composition) of contributions from constituent parts; this justifies treating spherical bodies as point-like under certain laws and underpins derivations of inverse-square behaviour for spheres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutuality and equality of gravitational action
rubrics_metrics.description: Gravitational action is mutual and equal (each body attracts the other equally): 'gravitatis actionem esse mutuam & utrinque aequalem' — this follows from thought-experiments about partitioning Earth's mass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept mutual gravitational action as a foundational axiom; use it to reason about center-of-mass effects and accelerations. Anti-pattern: asymmetric attraction assumptions are inconsistent with observed stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass-proportionality (gravitation proportional to quantity of matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: The force by which a body is attracted (its weight under a central attractor) is proportional to its quantity of matter (mass): 'pondera corporum... sunt ut quantitates materiae in corporibus.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use proportionality to mass when relating accelerative effects and composing forces; experimental confirmation invoked via equal acceleration of different masses in vacuum and pendulum experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse-square distance dependence of gravitational attraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Gravitational (centripetal) forces vary inversely as the square of the distance from the attracting center (deduced from lunar motion and planetary/cometary observations): 'hanc... proportionem... reciproce ut quadrata distantiarum.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A legitimate theory of celestial motion must produce (or be consistent with) an inverse-square law for centripetal attraction to match areas-in-time and observed orbital periods; computations (e.g., lunar fall vs terrestrial gravity) are cited as demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify centripetal (orbital) forces as directed to orbit centers and relate them to observable area law
rubrics_metrics.description: For bodies moving in planes, the force that causes area swept proportionality is one directed toward a fixed point (the center); hence planetary centripetal forces are toward the centers of their orbits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the geometric/mathematical relation between area law and central forces to deduce directionality of force. Practical implication: acceptance that planetary centripetal force acts toward the sun (or primary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory adequacy: the theory must account for multiple phenomena (planetary orbits, lunar motion, tides, comet paths, perturbations, apsidal precession)
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory physical theory should explain a broad set of phenomena (planetary revolutions, lunar inequalities, tides, cometary orbits, perturbations among planets); Newton’s work uses one set of principles to derive many such effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate theories by their ability to derive diverse observed phenomena from the same principles. Example: deriving tides and precession from lunar and solar gravitation is used as confirmation of the gravitational theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not posit imperceptible substances or properties unless necessary and demonstrable
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid assuming 'subtilissima materia' or occult properties that are neither perceived nor experimentally confirmed; if posited, their existence must be shown, not merely supposed to fit phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat suggestions of undetectable fluids/ethers skeptically; demand observational or experimental evidence before accepting such entities. Anti-pattern: invoking hidden fluids to 'explain' projectile parabolic motion without independent confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of astronomical phenomena (comets, planetary perturbations) to test the spatial extent and universality of forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations of comets (their large-range excursions) and planetary perturbations are used to infer that attractive forces extend to 'ingentes' distances and act universally on distant bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical tests should include long-range phenomena (comet orbits, perturbations between planets) to assess whether a proposed force law extends beyond local scales. The theory gains credibility if it explains both local (pendulum, fall) and long-range (comets, planetary interactions) data.
